title: Water supply holds on Courtland and Wimbleton developments
subtitle: Heritage designations including a downtown parking garage, 2026 audit plan, demolition approval, dangerous dog appeals, and Art Gallery anniversary.
overview: Council approved two development applications with holding provisions tied to the Region of Waterloo's water supply issue. At 808-836 Courtland Avenue East, a mixed-use project of up to 30 storeys and 977 dwelling units was approved {{vote:m1}}. At 7 Wimbleton Crescent, a zoning change was approved {{vote:m2}} that limits the site to two dwelling units until water capacity is confirmed, and caps building height at 10 metres. The Mayor said staff will keep reporting on how the Region's announcement affects planning approvals.

Council also moved ahead with heritage work, publishing a notice of intention to designate 160 Courtland Avenue East {{vote:m6}} and pursuing designation of seven more properties from the Bill 23 register review {{vote:m7}}. The 2026 internal audit work plan was approved {{vote:m4}}, and a demolition and rebuild at 26 Siebert Avenue was allowed {{vote:m11}}.

Council ratified two dog designation appeal decisions with modified conditions {{vote:m14}} {{vote:m15}}. The meeting opened with Girl Guide units leading O Canada and a presentation marking the Art Gallery's 70th anniversary.

decisions.detail: Council approved the Official Plan and zoning changes for a high-density mixed-use development of up to 30 storeys and 977 units, with a holding provision until water supply capacity is confirmed.
Council approved the rezoning with a holding provision limiting the site to two dwelling units until water capacity is confirmed, and a 10-metre maximum building height.
Council approved the 2026 Internal Audit work plan as outlined in the Chief Administrator's Office report.
Council directed the Clerk to publish a notice of intention to designate 160 Courtland Avenue East under the Ontario Heritage Act.
Council recognized the heritage value of seven properties, including the municipally owned parking garage at 33 Ontario Street North, and agreed to pursue their designation.
Council approved demolition of a single detached dwelling with an attached additional unit so it can be replaced with a new single detached dwelling.
Council ratified the appeal committee's decision upholding a dangerous dog designation, with modified conditions.
Council ratified the appeal committee's decision upholding a potentially dangerous dog designation, with modified conditions.

debate: A delegate living behind the Courtland site opposed the proposal, questioning the resident population estimate, the amount of parking, and the loss of commercial and industrial land. The delegate also raised traffic backups at Walton Avenue, Courtland and the expressway ramps.

One councillor agreed the site suits development but was concerned about traffic entering and leaving it. Staff said access would be worked out at site plan stage with the Region, which controls the road, and the Ministry of Transportation, because of the adjacent ramp.

On holding provisions, a councillor asked who can lift them. Staff said lifting one is a zoning by-law amendment decided by Council, once the Region confirms in writing that water capacity concerns are resolved. Staff said they would keep Council informed.

At Wimbleton Crescent, the applicant's consultant said the height measures 9.8 metres under the applicable zone rules and preferred no cap. A councillor proposed 10 metres anyway. Staff also answered nearby residents' flooding concerns, saying new construction must meet current grading and stormwater standards.

On the parking garage at 33 Ontario Street North, supporters cited city leadership on heritage and staff's view that designation can be reversed and allows routine maintenance. Opponents said it limits future use of the site and that the city's ownership already protects it.
